meta.title: How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big: Kind of the Story of My Life
meta.author: Scott Adams

parts.title: The Time I Was Crazy
parts.body: In 2005, Scott Adams was diagnosed with a mental illness by his doctor and a psychologist after he lost the ability to speak to humans, though he could speak normally to his cat or when alone. He declined Valium, not feeling crazy, but understood the diagnosis as his behavior appeared abnormal. His symptoms included his vocal cords clenching on certain consonants, making speech unintelligible, and a profound sense of loneliness from being unable to communicate. Adams, a professional speaker and syndicated cartoonist for Dilbert, faced a scheduled speaking event, risking humiliation in front of a thousand people. He informed his client and decided to go through with it to understand the pattern of his voice in that context.

parts.title: The Day of the Talk & Passion Is Bullshit
parts.body: The speaker faced a terrifying moment backstage before a talk, struggling to speak to organizers due to a voice problem. Despite his vast experience, he wondered if he could even deliver the speech. As he walked on stage, his heart pounded, but he managed to start speaking, though his voice was raspy. The audience loved his talk, but the moment he left the stage, his ability to speak vanished again, confirming the problem was in his brain. This experience fueled his three-year search for a solution, which forms the core of the book about turning failure into success. He then delves into the idea that passion is often misleading. He recalls his boss advising against lending money to passionate entrepreneurs, preferring those who work hard on spreadsheet-approved ventures. He hypothesizes that while passionate people might achieve huge successes, they also have many failures. He argues that success often *causes* passion, rather than the other way around. He also suggests that passion can simply be an indicator of talent, as people enjoy what they're good at.

parts.title: My Spectacular Failure and the Birth of My Systems Mindset
parts.body: In CHAPTER FIVE, the author made errors on the way to a job interview during a half-blizzard, going without a jacket and a suit and tie. The interviewer dismissed him for his attire. Driving home, his engine died in the Catskill Mountains in zero-degree Fahrenheit weather. Stranded without a jacket or cell phone, he faced a worst-case scenario. A traveling shoe salesman saved him, driving him back to campus. Months later, he traded his car for a one-way ticket to northern California, calling it his smartest decision. This near-death experience became his inspiration to move. He is grateful for the failure and no longer fears death outdoors. In CHAPTER SIX, the author flew to California for the first time at twenty-one, seeking success away from his hometown. He wore his first real suit for the flight, fearing denial for improper dress. On the plane, a CEO of a screw company offered career advice: always look for a better job, making job seeking an ongoing process. This was his first exposure to a system over a goal. The author learned appearance matters, as his suit earned him a potential job offer. Systems-driven people generally do better than goal-oriented people, who often feel a continuous sense of failure. He defines a goal as a specific, future objective and a system as a regular activity increasing long-term happiness. Systems have no deadlines and offer a more consistent path to success.

parts.title: From Corporate Conflict to Cartooning: The Power of Deciding, Enlightened Selfishness, and Energy Management
parts.body: The author discusses a workplace conflict where he applied company policy strictly regarding smoking, leading to a temporary walkout and the expectation of being fired. He highlights his attraction to controversy. Ultimately, his boss's boss intervened, making most offices smoke-free and requiring smokers in senior management to close their doors, a result the author considered ideal. Later, his career at Pacific Bell was hindered by a diversity policy preventing the promotion of white males, leading him to feel a sense of unwanted freedom and to explore new paths. This led him to cartooning, despite a lack of artistic talent. He started practicing drawing and using affirmations, specifically: "I, Scott Adams, will be a famous cartoonist." The author introduces Chapter Nine: Deciding Versus Wanting, emphasizing that success requires paying a price. He contrasts wishing with deciding, noting that deciding leads to action. He then introduces Chapter Ten: The Selfishness Illusion, arguing for enlightened selfishness as beneficial to society, citing examples like taxes and job creation. He provides permission to prioritize self-care, which ultimately benefits others. Finally, Chapter Eleven: The Energy Metric suggests organizing life around maximizing personal energy to better manage multiple priorities. He defines this as calm, focused energy and explains how it improves work quality, speed, and personal life, using the analogy of a "Dog Whisperer" for human interaction. He also contrasts simplifiers (like himself) with optimizers (like his wife Shelly), highlighting how simplification frees up time and energy, which he considers a "superpower" for his cartooning career. He concludes by recommending matching mental state to activity, using specific sitting positions for work, maintaining tidiness, and overcoming the fear of not knowing through quick research.

parts.title: The Asshole Lifestyle and Prioritizing Personal Energy
parts.body: Being an asshole can pollute group energy and is often seen as a lifestyle choice like "being yourself." However, this behavior can have a cost to your personal energy due to blowback and wasted effort in cleaning up messes. Many people adopt this "asshole lifestyle," and it's gender-inclusive, encompassing selfishness, arrogance, mean-spiritedness, and other flaws. The author defines an asshole as someone who unpleasantly impacts others' lives without productive or necessary reasons. Behaviors include changing the subject to oneself, dominating conversations, bragging, cheating, lying, disagreeing with everything, using honesty as cruelty, withholding favors, and abandoning civil behavior. Asshole behavior might feel good in the short term, like an addiction, but it's a bad long-term trade-off for personal well-being. The author suggests thinking of priorities in concentric circles: you (health) at the center, then economics (job, investments), followed by family, friends, and lovers. Outer rings include local community, country, and the world. The key is to manage inner circles before focusing on outer ones. Life isn't simple, and priorities overlap and conflict. A simple rule is to judge options by their influence on your personal energy: choices that make you stressed, unhealthy, and drained are likely wrong, while right choices usually charge you up. Meaningful work, even if demanding, can be energizing, unlike brain-deadening tasks. The author clarifies that priorities aren't about what you love most, but what you need to get right for the things you love to thrive. Even bad choices can temporarily energize, but long-term negative consequences are often obvious.

parts.title: My Speaking Career & The Path to Success
parts.body: A smart friend helped the author start a speaking career, advising him to ask for $5,000 for a speech, which was accepted along with first-class travel and hotel. As *Dilbert* grew popular, his speaking fees increased from $10,000 to $45,000, with one offer reaching $100,000. This success highlights the value of knowing different things from friends. After six months of losing his voice in 2005, and doctors being unable to diagnose it, the author turned to the Internet. He connected his previous hand problem to his voice issue, leading him to search for "voice dystonia." He found spasmodic dysphonia, a condition where vocal cords clench involuntarily, and a video confirmed his exact voice pattern. With a name, he found an expert doctor who confirmed the diagnosis but said there was no cure. The author, an optimist, saw this as a challenge to find his own cure. The author discusses how to recognize your talents and when to quit. Childhood obsessions (like his compulsive doodling) and tolerance for risk (like drawing inappropriate comics) can indicate natural aptitudes. Successful ventures often start out well and gain immediate traction. Strong reactions from a subset of the public (the "x factor") are a better predictor of success than average approval. If your work doesn't excite anyone, it's time to move on; if it does, be prepared to fight for it. The author critiques schools for not teaching systems of success, proposing a Success Formula: "Every Skill You Acquire Doubles Your Odds of Success." This means being "merely good" at multiple skills (Good + Good > Excellent). He sees himself as an example: mediocre art, business, and writing skills, combined with early Internet knowledge and a good sense of humor, became a powerful market force. Quantity often beats quality when it comes to skills.

parts.title: The Knowledge Formula: The More You Know, the More You Can Know
parts.body: The author emphasizes the importance of continuous learning and diversifying knowledge across various fields, likening new concepts to understanding a zebra after knowing what a horse is. He advocates for daily news consumption from diverse topics like business, health, and science to identify patterns and build a foundation for future learning. The key is to start with interesting topics to make news reading enjoyable, gradually expanding to other areas, making learning feel easy and natural. He cautions against dwelling on negative news, preferring stories about hopeful topics like green technology. The author reads news not for "truth" but to broaden exposure and make his brain more efficient, viewing it as a source of energy and optimism rather than just information.

parts.title: Business Writing and Accounting
parts.body: Learning business writing was a game-changer. It's all about getting to the point and cutting out unnecessary words and passive voice. These techniques make your writing clearer, more persuasive, and even funnier. For example, removing a word like “already” often doesn't change the meaning but makes the sentence stronger. Also, using direct writing (like “The boy hit the ball”) is much easier for the brain to process than passive constructions. Mastering these simple rules can make you seem smarter and more effective in communication. Accounting is crucial for being an effective adult, even if it seems boring. Understanding basic accounting concepts, like cash-flow projections and the time value of money, is part of the vocabulary of business. Many businesses fail because operators lack this fundamental understanding, prioritizing culinary skill over financial viability. Even if you pay others to handle accounting, you need enough knowledge to check their work and understand the basics to make informed decisions.

parts.title: Understanding Theory vs. Hypothesis & The Art of Persuasion
parts.body: This text distinguishes between theory and hypothesis, noting that a theory is a well-tested scientific explanation, while a hypothesis is an unproven idea. The author humorously admits to misusing "theory" in casual conversation, leading to public complaints. The text then transitions to the art of persuasion, emphasizing its importance in everyday interactions, whether in sales, personal relationships, or professional settings. The author suggests reading books on persuasion to understand its depth and effectiveness, highlighting it as a powerful skill that should be used judiciously and ethically. Key persuasive words and phrases are introduced, such as "Because" (which makes requests seem more reasonable), "Would you mind…?" (which signals a considerate request), "I’m not interested" (an effective conversation-stopper), and "I don’t do that" (a firm rule-like refusal). Other tactics include using "I have a rule…" to politely decline, "I just wanted to clarify…" to indirectly address difficult statements, and "Is there anything you can do for me?" to appeal to someone's helpful nature. The importance of a high-quality "Thank you", with specific details, is stressed, likening it to a dog treat that encourages future cooperation. Finally, sharing a non-dangerous secret with the phrase "This is just between you and me" is presented as a fast-track way to build trust and friendship.

parts.title: Happiness
parts.body: This chapter is about happiness. The author believes the only reasonable goal in life is to maximize your total lifetime experience of happiness. This isn't selfish, as normal people need to treat others well to be happy. Understanding what happiness is and how it works is crucial, similar to understanding gardening to grow a successful garden. Happiness is defined as a feeling from pleasant sensations produced by your body chemistry. It's not as dependent on circumstances as often thought; for example, amputees often return to their previous happiness levels. Everyone has a limited range of happiness, and life circumstances only jiggle them within that range. The good news is that most people can spend more time at the top of their personal range. The author treats himself like a "moist robot" and manipulates his body chemistry for happiness, which he sees as 80% of the solution. While pills and drugs can alter mood, he advocates a more natural approach. The biggest trick is being able to do what you want, when you want. Timing is more important than intrinsic value; a mediocre meal when starving is better than an extraordinary meal when full. Controlling your schedule is key, as flexibility contributes more to happiness than wealth. Parents understand this, as kids remove much schedule flexibility, impacting their happiness despite loving their children.

parts.title: Quitting Diet Coke and the Science of Eating
parts.body: The author used to consume a large amount of Diet Coke but decided to quit as an experiment for this book. The first week was challenging, but by substituting coffee, the need for willpower was greatly reduced. After eight weeks, the cravings were completely gone, and the author now feels more alert throughout the day. This experiment suggests that cravings can be managed and eliminated with a strategic approach, even for long-standing habits. Regarding healthy eating, the author emphasizes that it needs to be convenient to be sustainable. There's a lot of uncertainty in nutrition science, and what's considered healthy can change frequently. The author suggests using your body as a laboratory to test different foods and observe their effects on your energy and mood. This personal experimentation, combined with insights from science, can help you identify patterns that work best for your individual body.

parts.title: Vegetarianism, Coffee, and Fitness as Systems
parts.body: The author made a choice to be vegetarian, finding it easier in California than Kansas City. He feels lucky not to overeat and enjoys guilt-free treats. Being vegetarian is easier than it looks, despite initial inconveniences, because of feeling good physically. Coffee offers benefits like increased alertness, happiness, and productivity at two to four cups a day. It encourages exercise and contains antioxidants that reduce the risk of stroke, Parkinson's, and type 2 diabetes. Coffee makes him enjoy work without willpower, though caffeine addiction is a downside. The "Pleasure Unit Hypothesis" states that happier individuals care less about food taste, simplifying healthy eating. Getting your entire life in order helps maintain an ideal weight. The nine-point system for no-willpower dieting includes paying attention to energy levels, removing unhealthy food from home, and stocking convenient healthy options. Avoid addictive foods and eat healthy food freely. Get enough sleep, use fatty healthy foods for tiredness-induced hunger, choose low-calorie options for social eating, and season bland healthy foods. This system aims to lose cravings without sacrifice because willpower is a "losing strategy" for weight loss. The author advises to "Be Active Every Day" as a simple, effective approach to fitness that does not rely on willpower, as any exercise requiring it is unsustainable.

parts.title: A Final Note About Affirmations
parts.body: This chapter is about affirmations and how they appear to have a beneficial value, even if their mechanism isn't fully understood by science. The author acknowledges that some might see this as magic or psychic powers, but suggests they are likely a phenomenon of the mind, impacting psychology and perception. Affirmations could influence the brain through focus, motivation, or chemical reactions, similar to other forms of positive thinking like prayers or visualization. The author notes that in his experience, affirmations seem to have more power than simple positive thinking, creating an "illusion" that the world is changing to satisfy them. The author offers several explanations for the apparent power of affirmations: selective memory (remembering successes, forgetting failures), the possibility that people reporting success are liars (though he asserts he isn't), false memory (remembering events differently), and that optimists (who often practice affirmations) notice more opportunities than pessimists. He also suggests that perhaps only those who deep down believe in their talent bother with affirmations, or that our brains create illusions for survival benefits. He even touches on the idea of humans being holograms in a computer simulation, where affirmations could be a form of programming code. Ultimately, he reiterates that he has no objective information on their effectiveness but believes they involve a deep and consistent focus on what you want. He clarifies that affirmations, when viewed as a system for focus, optimism, and validation, are consistent with his "systems for winners" philosophy, recommending broad objectives.
